extracted.intended_audience: literate general readers and readers of 19th-century periodical literary criticism (Philadelphia Press audience)
extracted.subtask_description: An essay-style literary criticism and commentary (newspaper/periodical) addressing qualities of preaching, oratory, Shakespeare's plays, and Robert Burns — aimed at informing and persuading a general cultured readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sermon delivered without manuscript or notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Observes that Father Taylor's sermon had "no sign of any MS., or reading from notes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a virtue: spontaneous delivery implies authenticity and directness. Implied anti-pattern: reliance on manuscripts/notes can lessen immediacy and power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action, action, action (Demosthenean rule for speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: The old Demosthenean rule and requirement of "action, action, action," first in its inward and then (very moderate and restrain'd) its outward sense, was the quality that had leading fulfilment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Action means inward passion and moderately restrained outward expression; effective speeches combine inner urgency with controlled outward form. Scoring note: inward action is primary; excessive outward action is discouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colloquial style with Biblical/Oriental forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Father Taylor's talk was "Colloquial in a severe sense, it often lean'd to Biblical and Oriental forms."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A colloquial, conversational tone that nevertheless evokes Biblical or grand idioms can be powerful. Use of elevated allusion balanced with familiar speech is praised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of vivid, relevant imagery (ships/ocean)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allusions to ships and the ocean and sailors' lives were "of unrival'd power and life-likeness." The pulpit was backed by a mural of a stormy sea and ship in peril, contributing to effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagery rooted in the congregation's lived experience (here, sailors) amplifies persuasion. Setting and visual props that resonate with the audience are effective; anti-pattern: imagery irrelevant to listeners' world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impassioned, probing prayers that affect conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: The old man's prayers were "impassion'd pleading--such human-harassing reproach... probing to the very depths of that latent conscience and remorse."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective prayer (or emotional pleading) reaches and stirs listeners' consciences; rhetoric should fall away so that "live feeling" seizes the audience. Anti-pattern: mere rhetoric without genuine feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live feeling displacing mere rhetoric and art
rubrics_metrics.description: When Father Taylor preached or pray'd, "the rhetoric and art, the mere words... seem'd altogether to disappear, and the live feeling advanced upon you and seiz'd you with a power before unknown."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticity and felt emotion trump polished verbal artifice. Evaluation favors speakers whose emotional reality overwhelms crafted verbal technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsophisticated practices often strike deeper than trained elocution
rubrics_metrics.description: Questioning "why is it that the unsophisticated practices often strike deeper than the train'd ones?" and noting that minor local speakers often bring most definite results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naturalness and unrefined sincerity can be more effective than technically perfect elocution; teachers/pupils often undervalue this quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between oratory and elocution
rubrics_metrics.description: Oratory versus elocution: elocution (polish'd speaking) is relatively common, but "there seem to be few real orators--almost none."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elocution = cultivated technical skill; Oratory = rarer inner quality (passion, originality). When evaluating speakers, separate technical delivery from the deeper, rarer capacity for oratory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal electricity and atmosphere as part of effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator attributes being shaken by Father Taylor to "Father Taylor's personal electricity and the whole scene there--the prone ship in the gale, and dashing wave and foam for background."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A speaker's charisma and the surrounding atmosphere (visuals, setting) substantially influence impact. Assess both person and context together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical dramatic works may embody a controlling plan or ulterior design
rubrics_metrics.description: The English historical plays appear to be "the result of an essentially controling plan" and to carry "a lurking sense of being in aid of some ulterior design."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing historical plays, look for overarching structure, recurring themes, and possible political or ideological designs woven across multiple works; consider interpolations as possible devices to foil critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highest poetic nature hides and involves meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: A trait of highest poetic nature "causes it to cover up and involve its real purpose and meanings in folded removes and far recesses."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great poetry often conceals its deepest intentions; critics should expect layered, veiled meanings rather than plain statements. Anti-pattern: expecting transparent, single-level meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shakespeare's historical plays as portraits of feudal aristocracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakspere's historical plays "personify in unparallel'd ways the mediaeval aristocracy, its towering spirit of ruthless and gigantic caste" and depict feudal world and personalities vividly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate these plays for their sociological and political portraiture of feudalism; consider how characters and episodes reflect aristocratic mentality rather than mere dramatic skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great poems often arise from great historic perturbations
rubrics_metrics.description: The most distinctive poems "probably had their rise in the great historic perturbations, which they came in to sum up and confirm, indirectly embodying results to date."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a poet or cycle, consider its historical context and whether it crystallizes or responds to major societal upheavals; such origin explains form and enduring force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shakespeare's qualities: vast variety, delineation, sumptuousness, but also bombast and mannerism
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakspere's distinctiveness: "vast and rich variety of persons and themes, with his wondrous delineation of each and all... but great excess, superfoetation--mannerism... with boundless sumptuousness and adornment... but a good deal of bombast and fustian."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise Shakespeare for scope and character-crafting while acknowledging his excesses; critics should balance admiration for variety and richness against recognition of mannerism and rhetorical excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of works to modern democratic audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Whitman argues that Shakespeare (and other grand poets) are "mostly an objective and physiological kind of power" and that 'The comedies are altogether non-acceptable to America and Democracy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate literature for its resonance with contemporary democratic values: some classical works may embody aristocratic or monarchical sympathies less congenial to democratic societies. Use cultural relevance as one axis of judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burns's appeal rooted in personal life and 'errors'
rubrics_metrics.description: A large part of the fascination of Burns's songs is due to the poet's personal 'errors' and the "general bleakness of his lot" which fuse with his verses to create an "impalpable aroma."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess Burns not only on textual merits but on biographical merging with work; the authenticity of his life-story amplifies the songs' emotional force. Anti-pattern: judging Burns solely by canonical 'high art' standards without context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dialect, rawness, and unfinish as virtues in Burns
rubrics_metrics.description: Burns's use of Scotch patois and the 'native spice and untranslatable twang'—along with crudeness, haste, deficiencies, and 'unfinish'—are presented as consonant with his spirit and often pleasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value local idiom, roughness, and raw first drafts for their veracity and flavor; do not penalize lack of polish when it aligns with authentic voice. Scoring note: authenticity may outweigh formal perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burns's limitations: little spirituality, lack of large harmonies/complications
rubrics_metrics.description: Burns has "little or no spirituality... Harmonies, complications, oratorios in words, never." He 'did not know himself' and some motives are discreditable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When placing Burns in a literary hierarchy, note his melodic strengths and democratic charm but also his absence of philosophic/spiritual depth and elaborate structural mastery; these count as real limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patronage shaped poets' lives and could cause compromise
rubrics_metrics.description: The relation of patronage "cropped out a good deal in Burns's Letters" and "necessitated a certain flunkeyism... did as much as any one cause in making that life a chafed and unhappy one."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating poets of the era, consider economic/social constraints (patronage) as influencing content, tone, and career trajectory. Anti-pattern: treating works as if produced in autonomous solitude.
